The binding occupancy limiter is shared memory (Block Limit Shared Mem=6 vs Block Limit Registers=16, Block Limit Warps=16). The hardcoded R0_BLOCK=256 is over-provisioned for r0_numel=192 — 64 lanes (25%) are wasted per warp, inflating the shared memory footprint and preventing more blocks/SM. The correct approach is: (1) fix R0_BLOCK=192 to exactly match r0_numel=192, eliminating wasted lanes and reducing shared memory pressure, and (2) INCREASE XBLOCK to 256 or 512 so each block processes more x-rows per launch — this is the 'increase tile sizes' direction. With XBLOCK=256, grid=ceil(7840/256)=31 blocks but each block does more useful work; with XBLOCK=512, grid=16. The key insight is that the kernel is a per-row reduction (each x-index independently reduces over r0), so XBLOCK can be freely increased without correctness risk — larger XBLOCK means more rows per block, better L2 reuse of in_ptr2/in_ptr3 (which are indexed by r0_2 alone), and fewer kernel launches. Combined with R0_BLOCK=192, the shared memory per block drops, allowing more concurrent blocks per SM.

strategy_title: Halving num_warps worsens occupancy when grid is too small
strategy_description: Adding num_warps=2 configs to the autotune list caused the autotuner to select block_size=64 (half of the original 128), which halved the total thread count from 7936 to 3968 and cut waves_per_sm from 0.08 to 0.04. Although dynamic shared memory per block dropped from 32.77 KB to 16.38 KB (allowing Block Limit Shared Mem to rise from 6 to 13), the grid was already far too small (62 blocks on 132 SMs) to benefit — achieved occupancy actually fell from 6.23% to 3.12% because fewer total warps were launched. Memory throughput also collapsed from 326 GB/s to 137 GB/s, indicating the smaller block size reduced effective memory parallelism. When the grid is severely under-subscribed (<<1 wave/SM), reducing num_warps/block_size makes occupancy worse, not better — the shared memory savings are irrelevant when there are not enough blocks to fill the GPU.
applicable_when: Never — this strategy caused regression. Do not add num_warps=2 configs when grid_size << sm_count and waves_per_sm < 0.1.
do_not_apply_when: When the kernel grid is severely under-subscribed (grid_size < sm_count, waves_per_sm < 0.1). Reducing num_warps in this regime halves the total thread count, further reducing waves_per_sm and achieved occupancy. The shared memory savings from fewer warps are irrelevant when there are not enough blocks to fill the GPU. The autotuner will select the smaller num_warps config, making things worse.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_warps controls both the warp count per block and the block_size (block_size = num_warps * 32). Adding num_warps=2 to an autotune list where the grid is already too small will cause the autotuner to select it (lower shared memory = faster in microbenchmark), but the resulting halved thread count worsens real-world occupancy on under-subscribed grids.

strategy_description: Plan 'increase_xblock_tile_size_for_l2_cache_reuse' produced a kernel that crashed on execution after 4 attempt(s). Last error: kernel timed out after 60s
applicable_when: The kernel is catastrophically underutilized: 62 blocks on 132 SMs (0.04 waves), achieved occupancy 3.12% vs 40.6% theoretical. The autotune currently only explores XBLOCK=128 with varying num_warps/num_stages — it never tries larger XBLOCK values. Increasing XBLOCK to 256, 512, or 1024 means each block processes more x-rows per launch. Critically, in_ptr2 is indexed only by r0_2 (not x3), so with larger XBLOCK the in_ptr2 tile (294 floats = 1.2KB) stays resident in L2 across all rows in the block, improving reuse. Larger XBLOCK also reduces kernel launch overhead and grid scheduling overhead. R0_BLOCK MUST remain 256 (power-of-2 >= r0_numel=192) — all prior correctness failures occurred when R0_BLOCK was changed to non-power-of-2 values (192) or when XBLOCK was reduced. Increasing XBLOCK is safe: each program_id(0) independently owns a contiguous slice of x-rows, and the per-row reduction over r0 is self-contained within each block.

strategy_title: Adding num_warps=1 configs collapses occupancy on tiny grids
strategy_description: Adding num_warps=1 configs caused the autotuner to select block_size=32 (one warp per block), which reduced dynamic shared memory per block from 32.77 KB to 4.1 KB and raised theoretical occupancy from 37.5% to 50%. However, the total thread count collapsed from 7936 to 1984, cutting waves_per_sm from 0.08 to 0.01, and achieved occupancy fell from 6.23% to 1.56%. Memory throughput dropped from 324 GB/s to 88 GB/s because fewer concurrent warps could not hide memory latency. When the grid is severely under-subscribed (62 blocks on 132 SMs), reducing num_warps further shrinks the total warp count, making achieved occupancy worse regardless of theoretical improvements from shared memory savings.
applicable_when: Never — this strategy caused regression. Do not add num_warps=1 configs when grid_size << sm_count and waves_per_sm < 0.1.
do_not_apply_when: When the kernel grid is severely under-subscribed (grid_size < sm_count, waves_per_sm < 0.1). Reducing num_warps to 1 in this regime reduces block_size from 128 to 32, cutting total thread count by 4x and waves_per_sm from 0.08 to 0.01. The autotuner selects the smallest num_warps config because it has the lowest shared memory footprint in microbenchmark, but the resulting near-zero occupancy (1.56%) and collapsed memory throughput (88 GB/s vs 324 GB/s) make real-world performance far worse. The shared memory savings are irrelevant when there are not enough blocks to fill the GPU.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_warps controls both the warp count per block and the effective block_size (block_size = num_warps * 32). Adding num_warps=1 to an autotune list where the grid is already severely under-subscribed will cause the autotuner to select it due to minimal shared memory usage, but the resulting single-warp blocks cannot hide memory latency and achieved occupancy collapses. This is a more extreme version of the num_warps=2 regression observed in iteration 3 (item f3a2b891).

strategy_title: Remove reset_to_zero to unlock smaller XBLOCK autotune configs
strategy_description: When a Triton autotune decorator uses `reset_to_zero` on output pointers that have non-contiguous strides, the mechanism zeros the entire underlying storage buffer before each kernel launch. With small XBLOCK values, each block writes only a subset of output rows, but `reset_to_zero` zeros the entire buffer (including rows owned by other blocks that have not yet run), causing race conditions and catastrophically wrong results (max_diff in 1e8–1e11 range). Removing `reset_to_zero` is safe when the output pointers are written via direct `tl.store` (not atomic accumulation), because each store is idempotent and covers its own output region exactly once. Once `reset_to_zero` is removed, smaller XBLOCK configs (e.g., 16, 32, 64) become correct, dramatically reducing shared memory per block (from 32 KB to 16 KB at XBLOCK=16) and allowing the autotuner to select configs that cut kernel duration from 445 µs to 6.5 µs — a 69x speedup.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: reset_to_zero corrupts non-contiguous outputs with small XBLOCK
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
        # ... only XBLOCK=128 configs
    ],
    key=['xnumel', 'r0_numel'],
    reset_to_zero=['out_ptr0', 'out_ptr1'],  # zeros entire storage buffer!
    restore_value=['in_out_ptr0'],
)
# out_ptr0, out_ptr1 have non-contiguous strides (784, 1, 7840)
# small XBLOCK would zero rows owned by other blocks -> race condition
fast_pseudocode:
# AFTER: remove reset_to_zero, add small XBLOCK configs
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 16},  num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 16},  num_warps=8, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 32},  num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 32},  num_warps=8, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 64},  num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 64},  num_warps=8, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
        # ... more XBLOCK=128 configs
    ],
    key=['xnumel', 'r0_numel'],
    # reset_to_zero REMOVED: out_ptr0/out_ptr1 use direct tl.store, not atomics
    restore_value=['in_out_ptr0'],
)
# Autotuner selects XBLOCK=16 or 32: smem drops from 32KB to 16KB
# Duration: 445us -> 6.5us (69x speedup)
applicable_when: Triton kernel has `reset_to_zero` on output pointers that are written via direct `tl.store` (not atomic accumulation). The outputs have non-contiguous strides. The autotune only explores large XBLOCK values (e.g., 128) because smaller values previously caused correctness failures with max_diff in 1e8–1e11 range. The kernel is severely under-subscribed (grid_size << sm_count, waves_per_sm < 0.1) and shared memory is the binding occupancy limiter (Block Limit Shared Mem < Block Limit Registers and Block Limit Warps).
do_not_apply_when: Output pointers use atomic accumulation (e.g., tl.atomic_add) rather than direct tl.store — in that case, `reset_to_zero` is required for correctness. Also do not apply if the output pointers have contiguous strides, as `reset_to_zero` would only zero the exact elements being written and would not cause cross-block corruption. Do not remove `restore_value` for pointers that are read before being overwritten.
framework_notes: In Triton, `reset_to_zero` in `@triton.autotune` zeros the entire underlying storage tensor (not just the elements written by the current block) before each config trial. For non-contiguous tensors with strides like (784, 1, 7840), the storage buffer is much larger than the logical tensor, and zeroing it corrupts elements that belong to other blocks. This is a Triton-specific autotune mechanism with no direct equivalent in CUDA — in CUDA, you would manually zero buffers before kernel launch, which would have the same race condition if done incorrectly with partial-grid launches.

strategy_title: Cap registers via maxnreg and collapse arithmetic chains for FMA
strategy_description: Adding maxnreg=48 to Triton autotune configs alongside arithmetic chain collapsing (replacing 4-step sequential additions with a 2-step expression) reduced Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction from 26.3 to 19.41 cycles and kernel duration from 445 µs to 299 µs (1.5x speedup). The register cap (32→48 registers/thread, with stack size dropping from 8480 to 7232) reduced spill-related L1TEX stalls: CPIStall cycles from L1TEX dropped from 21.5 to 15.2 cycles per warp. Collapsing `tmp3=tmp1+tmp2; tmp4=tmp0+tmp3; tmp7=tmp5+tmp6; tmp8=tmp4+tmp7` into `tmp8 = tmp0 + (tmp1+tmp2) + (tmp5+tmp6)` reduced total executed instructions from 5.94M to 5.44M, enabling the compiler to emit fewer temporaries and more FMA-friendly instruction sequences.
slow_pseudocode:
# 4-step sequential addition chain (prevents FMA, inflates register count)
tmp3 = tmp1 + tmp2
tmp4 = tmp0 + tmp3
tmp7 = tmp5 + tmp6
tmp8 = tmp4 + tmp7
tmp9 = tl.broadcast_to(tmp8, [XBLOCK, R0_BLOCK])
# ...
tmp20 = tmp19 * tmp19  # non-fused multiply

@triton.autotune(configs=[
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=8, num_stages=1),
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=4, num_stages=2),
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=8, num_stages=2),
])
fast_pseudocode:
# Collapsed 2-step expression (enables FMA, reduces temporaries)
tmp8 = tmp0 + (tmp1 + tmp2) + (tmp5 + tmp6)
tmp9 = tl.broadcast_to(tmp8, [XBLOCK, R0_BLOCK])
# ...
tmp20 = libdevice.fma(tmp19, tmp19, tl.zeros_like(tmp19))  # explicit FMA hint

@triton.autotune(configs=[
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=4, num_stages=1, maxnreg=48),
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=8, num_stages=1, maxnreg=48),
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=4, num_stages=2, maxnreg=48),
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=8, num_stages=2, maxnreg=48),
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=8, num_stages=1),
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=4, num_stages=2),
    triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=8, num_stages=2),
])
applicable_when: Kernel has high CPIStall from L1TEX (>15 cycles/warp), high non-fused FP32 instruction fraction (>80%), and sequential arithmetic chains of 3+ additions that could be collapsed. Register count is elevated (>32 regs/thread) with stack spill activity (stack size >4KB). Grid is small and occupancy is already limited by shared memory, so maxnreg does not further reduce theoretical occupancy.
do_not_apply_when: When the kernel is already register-limited and maxnreg would force excessive spilling to local memory (indicated by high local load/store L2 miss rates). Also avoid when the arithmetic chain collapse changes floating-point associativity in ways that break numerical correctness requirements. Do not reduce maxnreg below 32.
framework_notes: In Triton, maxnreg is passed as a kwarg to triton.Config() and caps the maximum registers per thread for that config variant. The autotuner will select the best config including maxnreg variants. libdevice.fma(a, b, c) computes a*b+c as a fused operation; using tl.zeros_like(x) as the addend is a hint to emit fmul as FMA. maxnreg must be a multiple of 8 and >= 32. The equivalent in CUDA is __launch_bounds__(block_size, min_blocks_per_sm) or the maxrregcount PTX pragma.
